anchors.text: Accelerating charges radiate: Faraday + Ampère–Maxwell let the E and B fields regenerate each other, so the radiated field falls as 1/R (not 1/R²), is transverse (E ⊥ B ⊥ propagation), travels at 1/√(μ0ε0) = c, and has E = cB

Time and frequency domains are equivalent descriptions; a periodic wave is a sum of harmonics; line power ∝ amplitude², so amplitude ratios are square roots of power ratios (B10: 2.7:0.3:1.2 in power → 3:1:2 in amplitude)

authority.text: Non-dispersive medium assumed: λf = c holds only if speed is independent of f; in the ionosphere the group delay ∝ 1/f² (8.1 m at L1, 13.4 m at L2 for 50 TECU). The law λf = v stays; the value c fails
Infinite monochromatic plane wave: a real source gives a spherical 1/R wave, locally plane only in the far field; a finite pulse has bandwidth
Classical field picture: valid while the photon energy hf ≪ kT (10 GHz: 4.1e-5 eV vs kT 0.025 eV); breaks in the optical band (2.48 eV at 0.5 µm), where detectors count photons
c = 3e8 vs 299,792,458: +0.069% → 69 m bias at 100 km radar range; in air (n≈1.0003) 99 m; compare with a 150 m range cell for a 1 µs pulse
Mental rules λ[m] = 300/f[MHz], λ[cm] = 30/f[GHz]; 1 ns ↔ 30 cm; a 10 GHz period is 100 ps
Any shape f(z − vt) is a traveling wave; the constant-phase point gives v = ω/k = λf, and the sign of ωt sets the direction
The speed emerges from two electrical constants, 1/√(μ0ε0), measured with capacitors and coils: Maxwell's identification of light
λ sets the physical scale of the whole system: element size and spacing (~λ/2), aperture per beam, timing. Choosing a band means choosing λ
Borrowed structure (sonar): the same wave form holds for sound with c = 1500 m/s (10 kHz → 15 cm, the same λ as 2 GHz radio); the structure holds and only the medium constants change
Fighter-nose AESA: D≈0.7 m [estimate] at X band with λ/2 spacing → 1710 elements; at S band 154; published APG-81 ≈1,676 T/R modules [medium certainty] → back-solved D = 0.693 m
VHF surveillance radar at 170 MHz (λ = 1.76 m) needs very large antennas
authority.why: its meaning (beamwidth λ/D) is owned by lesson 3 / M1; mentioned in one clause of U40

authority.text: Using the free-space λ in coax (velocity factor 0.66): a 1 m cable at 1 GHz is 1818° of phase, not 1200°, which breaks phase matching
Letter-band ambiguity: EW 'C' = 0.5–1 GHz vs radar 'C' = 4–8 GHz; similar clashes for K and L
ω vs f (factor 2π), MHz vs GHz (factor 1000)
authority.why: not a separate exam question; it enters the exercises and the errorhunt (degree/radian slip) instead

authority.text: Phase is known only modulo 2π: with a baseline d > λ/2 there are several directions; d = 2λ and a measured 30° give 4 directions (−73.4°, −27.3°, 2.4°, 32.8°); the same issue is the GPS integer ambiguity
Phasors add only at the same frequency; with different f the relative phase rotates at Δω (a beat), the seed of Doppler
Superposition needs a linear medium and linear devices; it fails in a saturated front end (intermodulation) and is exploited in a mixer
Phasor for a non-steady signal: narrowband (slowly varying envelope) approximation
Angle sensitivity δθ = δφ/(k d cosθ): 10° of phase error at d = λ/2 → 3.18° at broadside and 3.68° at 30°, growing toward endfire
1° of phase = λ/360: 83 µm at 10 GHz, 0.53 mm at GPS L1, 1.39 nm at 0.5 µm
Rotating arrow: a cosine is the projection of a rotating phasor; same-frequency sums are vector sums, the result is again a sinusoid at that frequency, and the time factor drops out
Multiplying complex numbers multiplies magnitudes and adds angles, so a delay or path is multiplication by e^{jΔφ}
Relative phase across space gives angle (arrays, interferometers), across time gives velocity (Doppler, M2), across frequency gives range; it needs a coherent reference
Coherent sum of equal in-phase waves gives +6 dB, incoherent +3 dB
GPS carrier phase: λL1 = 19.03 cm; C/A chip 293 m = 1540 λ; 1% of a cycle = 1.9 mm vs 1% of a chip = 2.93 m; integer ambiguity; RTK ≈ 1 cm + 1 ppm
Wideband EW interferometer 2–18 GHz: a λ/2 baseline at 18 GHz (8.33 mm) is only 0.056 λ at 2 GHz, about 9× poorer phase sensitivity → several baselines
Sign-convention clash: B02 cos(kz−ωt+φ) (+φ = later peak at fixed z), B10 (+ = advanced), Driggers cos(2πνt−φ) with e^{jkz}; mixing them mirrors a steering angle
Calculator in degree mode vs radians inside sin: 98.5° becomes 262.9°
Adding powers when phasors should be added
Energy conservation: power through a sphere ∝ E²·4πR² is constant only if E ∝ 1/R; this is S = ERP/4πR² from M0.1
Near-field terms relative to the radiation term ~1/(kR); crossover at R = λ/2π: 4.77 mm at 10 GHz, 15.9 m at 3 MHz; at 10λ −36 dB
Magnetic/electric force on a charge in a wave = v/c; an electron in 1 V/m at 1 GHz: v ≈ 28 m/s, v/c ≈ 9.3e-8 → receivers sense E
Reading a power spectrum as amplitude (9:1:4 instead of 3:1:2) or taking 10 log of an amplitude
dB consistency: power 0.3/2.7 → −9.54 dB = 20 log(1/3); 32 Hz line −3.52 dB
A power spectrum discards phase: the same three tones with different phases give different time waveforms and the same spectrum

parts.covers: plan block; story: Hertz in Karlsruhe 1886–88 (standing waves, measured λ × computed f ≈ c, wire-grid polarization test; Poincaré's √2 correction to the computed frequency). Problem/why-hard/idea paragraphs (in M0.1 we used ERP/4πR², E⊥B and |E|/|B| = c as given; now we derive them). History block on Maxwell 1861–65. Tool-building: vectors, dot product (flux), cross product (right-hand rule), each in a definition block before use. Lorentz force (A.1) B02:930 with the v/c ratio. Table A-1 in words, Table A-2 integral form explained as flux/circulation (B02:930–931). Displacement current step. Radiation from an accelerating charge: 1/R² vs 1/R (B02:930–931), energy-conservation proof, kink/sinθ, near-field crossover λ/2π vs 2D²/λ. Wave equations (A.3), c = 1/√(μ0ε0) with compute (A.2); substitution step with a curvature intuition for the second derivative (formal derivative deferred, said explicitly). Transversality from Gauss; TEM and Fig 1-2 (B02:42–43) with the sign check E +y → B −x; E = cB from Faraday on a small loop; Z0 = 376.73 Ω closing the M0.1 promise; footnote B vs H (B02:42). Erratum at the end of the section: ∇² is the Laplacian, not a gradient (B02:931); OCR 'c 3×1o°' (B02:42); 'a electromagnetic' (B02:930).

results.text: The traveling plane wave E = E0 cos(kz − ωt + φ), with k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf, phase speed v = ω/k, and λf = c in vacuum (λf = c/n in a medium)
results.thread: Given a carrier frequency, what physical length scale (wavelength) and time scale does the wave impose on every antenna, cable, timing and ranging calculation, and how far can the vacuum value c be trusted?

results.text: Phase and the phasor: complex amplitude u = a·e^{jφ}; a plane wave in a general direction u = A·e^{jk(γx x+γy y+γz z)}; path-induced phase difference Δφ = kγΔz (across a baseline d: Δφ = k d sinθ); same-frequency superposition is the complex sum of phasors
results.thread: How do we calculate what two receivers, two paths or two waves of the same frequency produce together, and how precisely can a measured phase difference give angle or distance?

plan.title: הגל האלקטרומגנטי: ממשוואות מקסוול לגל נע, אורך גל, תדר, פאזה ופאזור

units.q: Hertz measured λ and computed f. What does an error in f do to the inferred speed, and what independent check catches it?
units.text: Hertz 1886–88: standing-wave λ × computed LC frequency ≈ c; √2 frequency-calculation error

units.q: Why was a speed computed from capacitor and coil measurements evidence that light is an electromagnetic wave?
units.text: Maxwell 1861–65: displacement current; 1/√(μ0ε0) from bench constants ≈ speed of light

units.q: Define the dot product and explain why only the field component normal to the surface counts in the flux.
units.text: Vector, components, dot product as projection; flux uses E·dA

units.q: Give the magnitude and direction of a×b; what is ŷ×x̂?
units.text: Cross product: magnitude |a||b|sinθ, direction by the right-hand rule

units.q: Write the Lorentz force, define every symbol, and say which term does no work and why.
units.text: Lorentz force F = q(E + v×B) defines the fields by their force

units.q: Estimate the magnetic-to-electric force ratio on an electron in a 1 V/m, 1 GHz wave. Why do we track only E?
units.text: In a wave F_mag/F_el = v/c ≈ 1e-7: receivers sense E

units.q: State the four laws in words and which pair couples E and B in time.
units.text: Maxwell's four laws in words (Table A-1)

units.q: Define flux and circulation in words and give the law that uses each.
units.text: Flux through a closed surface; circulation around a loop (Table A-2)

units.q: At which step is Maxwell's term needed, and what inconsistency appears without it?
units.text: Displacement current fixes Ampère's law for a charging capacitor

units.q: Why does the mutual regeneration of E and B change the decay law from 1/R² to 1/R?
units.text: Gauss+Ampère alone: fields ∝ 1/R²; with induction terms: radiated fields ∝ 1/R

units.q: Prove with power flow that a radiated field must fall as 1/R. What would 1/R² imply at 10 km vs 1 km?
units.text: Energy flow through a sphere forces E ∝ 1/R; this is ERP/4πR²

units.q: Why doesn't a DC current radiate, and in which direction does an oscillating charge not radiate?
units.text: Acceleration, not velocity, radiates; transverse kink ∝ a·sinθ/R; no radiation along the axis

units.q: Estimate where the near-field terms equal the radiation term at HF and at X band; how small is the near-field term at 10λ?
units.text: Near-field/radiation crossover at R = λ/2π: 4.77 mm at 10 GHz, 15.9 m at 3 MHz

units.q: A 3 m dish at 10 GHz: which far-field distance governs a pattern measurement and why?
units.text: λ/2π (source physics) vs 2D²/λ (aperture phase): different far-field criteria

units.q: What do the vacuum wave equations predict for the speed, and from which constants?
units.text: Free-space wave equations (A.3); speed 1/√(μ0ε0) = 299,792,458 m/s

units.q: Show why a cosine satisfies the wave equation only if ω/k = c.
units.text: Substituting cos(kz−ωt): curvature k² vs ω²μ0ε0 → ω/k = c

units.q: Using the flux through a box, why can't a vacuum plane wave have an E component along its propagation direction?
units.text: Gauss's law on a thin box forbids a longitudinal E in a vacuum plane wave

units.q: With E along +y and propagation along +z, in which direction is B at that instant? Check it with E×B.
units.text: TEM: E ⊥ B ⊥ v; E×B along v; E +ŷ ⇒ B −x̂ for +z

units.q: Derive E0 = cB0. At which step does 'the pattern moves at c without changing shape' enter?
units.text: E = cB from Faraday on a small loop plus the traveling-pattern condition

units.q: Derive Z0 from E = cB and H = B/μ0, and give its value.
How does the 1/R field law explain the one-way 20 log R of an EW receiver measuring dBµV/m?
units.text: EW listener's 20 log R is exactly the 1/R radiated field

units.q: Define a wave and propagation; what carries the information?
units.text: Wave: a disturbance moving while keeping its shape, carrying information in its parameters

units.q: Define the radian and convert 1 rad; what error does the 60° shortcut carry?
units.text: Radian = arc/radius; 2π rad = 360°; 57.3°/rad; ≈60° is 4.7% high

units.q: For B10's example, read off the amplitude and wavelength and explain why the amplitude is 0.5.
units.text: Sinusoid parameters: amplitude (half of peak-to-peak), wavelength (Figs 1-2, 1-3)

units.q: Write the traveling-wave expression, define every symbol, and give the conditions under which it holds.
units.text: E = E0 cos(kz − ωt + φ), k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf

units.q: Derive k = 2π/λ from the snapshot view.
units.text: t fixed: the cosine repeats when kz advances 2π → k = 2π/λ (Fig 1-3)

units.q: Derive ω = 2πf from the fixed-point view.
units.text: z fixed: period T0, f = 1/T0, ω = 2π/T0 (Fig 1-4)

units.q: Which way does cos(kz + ωt) travel? Derive its speed.
units.text: Constant phase kz − ωt = const ⇒ v = ω/k = λf; sign sets direction

units.q: Derive λf = c from v = ω/k and compute f for λ = 3 cm.
units.text: λf = c (vacuum); 3 cm ⇒ 10 GHz

units.q: In your head: λ at 150 MHz, 1.3 GHz and 35 GHz (2 m, 23 cm, 8.6 mm).
units.text: λ[m] = 300/f[MHz]; λ[cm] = 30/f[GHz]; 1 ns ↔ 30 cm

units.q: Estimate the range bias at 100 km from using 3e8, in vacuum and in air; when does it matter against a 150 m cell?
units.text: c = 3e8 is 0.069% high: 69 m bias at 100 km; 99 m in air

units.q: Which assumption hides in λf = c, where does it break for GPS, and what survives (λf = v)?
units.text: λf = c assumes a non-dispersive vacuum; ionosphere breaks it (L1 8.1 m, L2 13.4 m)

units.q: Define dispersion and explain why a prism separates colors; which color bends more?
units.text: Dispersion: speed depends on frequency; a prism separates colors (Fig 1-6)

units.q: What is imprecise in calling fλ = c 'the dispersion relationship', and how should it be phrased?
units.text: fλ = v always holds; the dispersion relation is ω(k); fλ = c is the non-dispersive case

units.q: When is the infinite plane cosine a valid model of a radar wave at the target, and what replaces it near the antenna or for a short pulse?
units.text: Plane monochromatic idealization: locally plane in the far field; a pulse has bandwidth

units.q: Why is a radio wave treated as a classical field and visible light at the detector as photons? Give the numbers.
units.text: Classical wave valid while hf ≪ kT: 4.1e-5 eV at 10 GHz vs 2.48 eV at 0.5 µm

units.q: Give the wavelength span of the L, S, X and Ka bands without a calculator.
units.text: Radar band wavelengths (Table 1-1): HF 100–10 m … X 3.75–2.5 cm … W 4–2.7 mm

units.q: Why does a radar use only an ITU slice of its band, and why are frequencies above 16 GHz picked at absorption nulls?
units.text: Radars span 3 MHz–300 GHz, mostly 0.3–35 GHz; ITU slices; >16 GHz at absorption nulls

units.q: A spec says 'C band receiver'. What two readings exist, and how do you state it unambiguously?
units.text: EW letters ≠ radar letters: EW C = 0.5–1 GHz vs radar C = 4–8 GHz

units.q: Moving a radar from S to X band with the same aperture: what changes in element count and hardware scale?
units.text: λ sets the physical scale: element spacing ~λ/2, aperture per beam, timing

units.q: Estimate the element count of a 0.7 m X-band aperture, compare it with the published value, and explain the gap.
units.text: Fighter AESA: 0.7 m aperture, λ/2 → 1710 elements at X, 154 at S; APG-81 ≈1,676

units.q: What do you gain and pay, and how much, when you double the frequency of a fixed-size array?
units.text: Higher f: more elements per aperture (∝f²) vs cost, cooling and rain/atmospheric loss

units.q: An engineer phase-matches cables using λ = c/f. What is wrong, and how big is the error for a 1 m, VF 0.66 cable at 1 GHz?
units.text: Free-space λ used in coax: 1 m at 1 GHz is 1818°, not 1200°

units.q: How does c enter a radar's range measurement, and what range corresponds to 1 µs?
units.text: Radar ranging R = cΔT/2 (Fig 1-1 chain); 1 µs ↔ 150 m

units.q: What carries over from the EM wave to sonar, and what differs (medium, speed variability)?
units.text: Sonar: same wave form, c = 1500 m/s; 10 kHz → 15 cm

units.q: How does a dual-frequency GPS receiver turn dispersion into a measurement?
units.text: GNSS dual frequency: delay ∝1/f², ratio 1.647 → ionosphere-free solution

units.q: Define the phase and the initial phase; why is k called a spatial frequency?
units.text: Phase = total argument kz − ωt + φ; initial phase φ; k as spatial frequency

units.q: Why is a single wave's phase meaningless while the phase between two waves is measurable?
units.text: Absolute phase is arbitrary and unmeasurable; relative phase is physical

units.q: List the four ways two waves can get out of phase; convert 50° at 10 GHz into time and path.
units.text: Relative phase from k, f, φ or path; 50° at 10 GHz = 13.9 ps = 4.17 mm

units.q: State B10's sign convention and why −φ and 360° − φ are the same shift.
units.text: Advanced = positive shift; −φ ≡ 360° − φ (Fig 1-5)

units.q: In B02's cos(kz − ωt + φ), does +φ make the peak at a fixed z come earlier or later? How do you check a source's convention?
units.text: Three sign conventions (B02, B10, Driggers); mixing them mirrors steering

units.q: What engineering problem did Steinmetz's complex method solve, and what assumption (single steady frequency) did it require?
units.text: Euler's formula (1748); Steinmetz (1893) turned AC differential equations into algebra

units.q: Define a complex number, its magnitude and angle, and e^{jφ}.
units.text: Complex number a+jb, magnitude, angle; e^{jφ} = cosφ + j sinφ

units.q: Why is a path delay represented as multiplication by e^{jΔφ}?
units.text: Multiplication multiplies magnitudes and adds angles: a delay is ×e^{jΔφ}

units.q: Define the phasor and recover the real wave from it; why does Driggers write u* in (4.3)?
units.text: Phasor u = a e^{jφ}; real wave = Re{u e^{jωt}} (Driggers' conjugate form)

units.q: Why is the sum of two same-frequency sinusoids again a sinusoid at that frequency? Show it with phasors.
units.text: Rotating arrow: the cosine is a projection; same-f sums close to the same f

units.q: Derive the time average of the squared wave from the phasor, and connect it to the effective field.
units.text: Time average ⟨u²⟩ = ½|u|²; links to E_eff = E_peak/√2 (3.01 dB)

units.q: Why does an IR/visible detector measure power only while a radio receiver can keep phase?
units.text: Optical detectors cannot follow 600 THz: they measure irradiance and lose the phase

units.q: Define a wavefront and its relation to the propagation direction in an isotropic medium.
units.text: Wavefront = constant-phase surface; plane wave Ae^{jkz}; fronts λ apart (Fig 4.2)

units.q: Write the plane wave in a general direction and prove that the direction cosines satisfy Σγ² = 1.
units.text: u = A e^{jk(γx x+γy y+γz z)}; γ = cosθ; Σγ² = 1

units.q: Derive the phase difference between two receivers spaced d for a wave arriving at θ from broadside.
units.text: Δφ = kγΔz; across a baseline Δφ = k d sinθ; λ/2 at 30° → 90°

units.q: Why may the z-phase factor be dropped in the image plane, and what information remains in the transverse phase?
units.text: (4.9b): the constant z-phase drops out; the transverse phase gradient carries direction

units.q: Estimate the angle error from a 10° phase error with d = λ/2 at broadside and at 30°; how does it scale with d and θ?
units.text: δθ = δφ/(k d cosθ): 10° gives 3.18° at broadside, 3.68° at 30°

units.q: Which hidden assumption does Δφ → θ rely on, when does it break, and what survives?
units.text: Phase known mod 2π: d = 2λ, 30° measured → 4 directions

units.q: Choose a baseline for unambiguous ±60° (d < 0.577λ, 1.73 cm at 10 GHz) and explain the trade with precision.
units.text: Long baseline: precision ∝ 1/d, ambiguities ≈ 2d/λ; coarse+fine baselines

units.q: Define superposition as a phasor sum and give the in-phase and out-of-phase cases.
units.text: Superposition: same f, same place and time → complex sum; constructive or destructive

units.q: Where does superposition stop holding in a receiver, and what appears instead?
units.text: Superposition needs linearity; fails in a saturated front end (intermodulation)

units.q: Two waves at 10.000 and 10.001 GHz: can they be added as fixed phasors? What does the sum do in time?
units.text: Phasor sum only at the same f; otherwise a relative phase rotating at Δω (beat)

units.q: When can a pulsed signal still be described by a phasor, and what replaces it when it can't?
units.text: Phasor for pulses: slowly varying envelope (narrowband) approximation

units.q: Estimate the path length per degree of phase at GPS L1 and at 10 GHz.
units.text: 1° = λ/360: 83 µm at X band, 0.53 mm at L1, 1.39 nm optical

units.q: Compare carrier-phase and code ranging precision at 1% of a cycle/chip; what must be solved to use it?
units.text: GPS carrier phase: λ 19.03 cm vs chip 293 m (1540×); RTK cm

units.q: What system measurements does relative phase enable, and what hardware requirement follows?
units.text: Phase across space → angle, across time → velocity, across frequency → range; needs coherence

units.q: Why does a wideband DF interferometer need several baselines?
units.text: 2–18 GHz interferometer: 8.33 mm baseline is 0.056λ at 2 GHz

units.q: Define both domains and spectral decomposition; in what sense are they equivalent?
units.text: Time-domain vs frequency-domain descriptions; spectral decomposition

units.q: Sketch the spectrum of a pure 8 Hz cosine.
units.text: 8 Hz cosine: 8 cycles per second ↔ one line at 8 Hz (Fig 1-7)

units.q: What is a harmonic, and why does a periodic non-sinusoidal wave contain only multiples of its fundamental?
units.text: Periodic wave = harmonics; 8, 16, 32 Hz (Fig 1-8)

units.q: From line powers 2.7, 0.3 and 1.2, derive the amplitude ratios.
units.text: Power ∝ amplitude²: 2.7:0.3:1.2 → 3:1:2

units.q: Express the 16 and 32 Hz lines in dB relative to 8 Hz using power and using amplitude.
units.text: dB consistent: 10 log(0.3/2.7) = 20 log(1/3) = −9.54 dB; −3.52 dB

units.q: An analyst reads 9:1:4 as amplitudes from Fig 1-8. What is wrong, and which check catches it?
units.text: Reading power as amplitude gives 9:1:4; check the axis units and Parseval

units.q: Why is 'power density (W/Hz)' an imprecise label for the lines of a periodic signal?
units.text: Discrete lines are powers (W), not densities (W/Hz)

units.q: Two signals have identical power spectra. Must they look the same in time? Why?
units.text: A power spectrum discards phase: same tones, different waveforms

units.q: Find the planted error in an AI phase-difference computation and name the check that catches it.
units.text: Errorhunt: sin(20) in radians: 262.9° instead of 98.5°
